title: 3-Read Friday #75: Silence, Attention, and Reflective Practice
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #75 links three posts that share a concern for the teacher's own restraint, awareness, and self-reflection as levers on classroom quality. Adam Robbins opens with a short, punchy 'quick-hitters' post arguing that once a teacher has set students working in silence, the single most damaging thing they can do is break that silence themselves - silence, once broken, is hard to re-establish. Mike Hobbiss offers a deep, research-grounded case that classroom attention is not just a pedagogical nicety but a social-justice issue: studies show that engaging students' attention through cueing can neutralise the apparent effects of IQ and socioeconomic status on memory performance, meaning that failing to systematically cue attention disproportionately disadvantages students who most need it. Chris Shore, a mathematics PGCE tutor at Loughborough University, presents a framework for reflective practice grounded in models like Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle and Gibbs' Reflective Cycle, aimed at helping teachers of any experience level turn daily classroom experiences into deliberate professional growth. Barton's own commentary frames all three as practical, research-informed tools for teachers seeking to be more deliberate about what they do - and don't do - in the classroom.
points: Adam Robbins's core message: once silence is established for independent work, breaking it yourself as the teacher is often the single biggest threat to it - 'give and inch and they take a mile.'

Mike Hobbiss's central research finding: attention-cueing studies show that when children's attention is actively engaged, the usual correlations between IQ and memory performance, and between socioeconomic status and memory performance, largely disappear.

Hobbiss's framing this as a social-justice issue: if cueing attention can neutralise the disadvantage associated with lower SES, then a school's failure to systematically cue attention becomes an equity problem, not just a pedagogical one.

Chris Shore's reflective-practice framework draws on established models (Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle, Gibbs' Reflective Cycle) to give PGCE trainees and experienced teachers alike a structured way to turn daily classroom experience into deliberate growth.

A shared thread Barton draws across the issue: each post asks teachers to be more deliberate about an aspect of practice easy to overlook - restraint (silence), attentional design (cueing), and structured reflection (professional growth).
quotes: A short post with an important message: sometimes the best thing we can do as teachers is shut up.
